query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a thin copper layer before composite consolidation will improve the tungsten–copper interfacial bonding and reduce electronic scattering at the interface, thereby enhancing the overall thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite while maintaining its mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu metal-matrix composite prepared via powder metallurgy in which tungsten particles are used in their as‐received (uncoated) form.
generation.intervention: Apply an ultrathin, uniform copper coating (e.g., via electroplating or sputter deposition) onto tungsten particles prior to composite consolidation.
generation.conditions: The composite will be consolidated (e.g., by powder metallurgy or spark plasma sintering) and then tested under conditions representative of fusion-reactor joint applications: high heat flux at moderate-to-high temperatures (e.g., 300–500 °C) and exposure to relevant irradiation (e.g., He implantation or simulated neutron irradiation) while subject to mechanical loads.
generation.structural_mediator: The pre-coated tungsten particles form a seamless, compositionally compatible interphase with the copper matrix that alleviates mismatches in lattice structure and work function. This reduced interfacial thermal resistance mediates enhanced electronic conduction across the particle boundaries.
generation.mechanism: By eliminating or reducing the interfacial discontinuities that normally scatter conduction electrons, the copper coating facilitates more efficient electron transport from the high-conductivity copper matrix into and out of the tungsten inclusions. This improved electron path reduces thermal resistance at the interface without altering the microstructural reinforcement that imparts mechanical durability and irradiation tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a standard W–Cu composite with uncoated tungsten particles, the pre-coated composite is expected to show a measurable increase in thermal conductivity while retaining similar mechanical strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: A W–Cu composite produced under identical processing conditions but using uncoated tungsten particles.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected only if the copper coating is uniformly thin (on the order of tens of nanometers) and does not become so thick as to introduce undesirable intermetallic phases or compromise particle–matrix bonding; furthermore, irradiation must not degrade the integrity of the coating.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum coating thickness and deposition method must be determined experimentally, and the long-term stability of the copper interphase under fusion-relevant irradiation conditions remains to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites using an identical powder metallurgy route. Set A uses tungsten particles pre-coated with a ~20–30 nm copper layer (applied via sputtering or electroplating), while Set B uses uncoated tungsten particles. Process both sets under the same sintering conditions. Subject the samples to high thermal flux (e.g., 300–500 °C heating cycles) and controlled irradiation (e.g., He+ implantation at reactor-relevant energies) followed by mechanical testing.
measurements: Thermal conductivity measurements via laser flash analysis.
Mechanical durability tests (e.g., tensile/compressive strength, fracture toughness).
Microstructural and interfacial characterization via SEM/TEM before and after irradiation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the copper-coated composite (Set A) does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity over the uncoated composite (Set B) or if its mechanical durability or irradiation resistance is degraded beyond an acceptable margin (compared to Set B), the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The requirement of innovative plasma-facing and high-temperature materials has turned researchers’ attention towards refractory metals due to their high-temperature properties, such as a high melting temperature, good strength, and good creep resistance. Intensive research has explored the properties and performance of tungsten in plasma-facing applications, , . A unique combination of various physical, chemical, mechanical and irradiation characteristics, including a high melting temperature, good thermal conductivity, a proper sputtering threshold, , good creep strength, a low level of tritium retention, and neutron activation and erosion have made W a potential material for plasma-facing components of fusion reactors, . Although the potential of W for use as a plasma-facing material is accepted, its commercial roles remain restricted due to its high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT), radiation-induced embrittlement, its low yield strength and the fact that it oxidizes readily at elevated temperatures into WO3, which is volatile above ~1000 °C, , , . Thermonuclear fusion is a novel technology for clean and economical energy production associated with several environmental benefits. The technological challenges are under intensive research and development in order to have fusion power in full performance for energy production by the 2050s. One key challenge is related to the extreme conditions required for the fusion reactions, as hydrogen isotopes fuse in high temperatures under high magnetic fields and pressures and produce high fluxes of neutron and electromagnetic radiation. The conditions are demanding for the materials covering the plasma-facing wall of the reactor, and the ability of wall material to withstand this environment is a key issue for long-term energy production []. The current choices of materials for the first wall of the next-step fusion device ITER are beryllium and tungsten. Tungsten has good thermal conductivity, high sputtering resistance and low erosion yield, and retention of hydrogenic species in bulk W is low.
